summary: Defines terms used when measuring the performance of firewalls, extending the vocabulary already used for benchmarking routers and switches. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2647 defines terms for describing firewall performance. It explains what to count as forwarded traffic and how to describe connections so that benchmark results can be compared consistently.

questions: what is a dmz in networking
subtitle: Definitions for comparing firewall forwarding and connection performance.

tldr.problem: Firewall designs vary, making performance comparisons difficult without shared definitions for traffic, forwarding and connections.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines firewall benchmarking terms and extends terminology used for routers and switches, including bit forwarding rate, goodput and concurrent connections.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2647 supplies definitions, not a test procedure, and warns that performance choices can conflict with security safeguards.

today: RFC 2647 is an Informational memo published in August 1999, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines benchmarking terminology and does not specify a test methodology.

sections.title: Why Firewall Benchmark Terms Matter
sections.content:
The memo defines vocabulary for measuring firewall performance and extends terminology already used for benchmarking routers and switches. It focuses on forwarding rate and measurements related to connections.

The author cites three reasons for defining these terms: no standard measurement method, wide variation among implementations, and uncertainty about whether a firewall can handle heavy loads on faster internal networks. The memo adopts the definition format used by RFC 1242 and directs readers to the router and switch terminology documents as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Firewall products can be difficult to compare because they may handle traffic differently. Shared definitions help testers describe what they measured.

sections.title: Traffic Classes and Rule Sets
sections.content:
A firewall enforces an access-control policy between networks through a rule set. The memo distinguishes allowed traffic, which the rule set permits and the firewall forwards; rejected traffic, which the firewall actually drops; and illegal traffic, which the rule set says should be rejected whether or not the firewall drops it.

This distinction matters when measuring performance. Bit forwarding rate includes allowed traffic forwarded to the correct destination interface. Rejected packets are not included, and illegal traffic may reveal a faulty or misconfigured firewall if it is forwarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo separates traffic the rules allow, traffic the firewall actually drops and traffic the rules say should be dropped. A benchmark must keep these categories distinct.

sections.title: Firewall Designs and Network Segments
sections.content:
The memo defines packet filtering as checking packet headers against rules, and stateful packet filtering as checking packets against connection state kept by the firewall. A circuit proxy statically forwards traffic allowed by its rules. An application proxy is set up in response to a client request and forwards packets only after a connection has been established.

A protected network is controlled by the firewall; an unprotected network is not. A demilitarized zone (DMZ) lies between them and may contain public servers. A firewall with three network interfaces is tri-homed. The memo defines these terms to identify which network layout and firewall behavior a test describes.
sections.plainLanguage: Firewalls can check packet headers, track connection state or proxy connections. Terms such as protected network, DMZ and tri-homed describe the networks and interfaces involved.

sections.title: Forwarding Rate and Connection Measures
sections.content:
Bit forwarding rate is the number of bits per second of allowed traffic that the firewall forwards to the correct destination interface for a specified offered load. The memo treats it as goodput: lost or retransmitted bits are not counted. A unit of transfer is a discrete collection of bytes with at least one header, such as a TCP segment, IP packet or Ethernet frame; testers must state which unit they use and compare like units.

The memo also defines concurrent connections, connection establishment and teardown times, and connection overhead. A connection is a state in which hosts, or a host and firewall, agree to exchange data; for firewall performance, a UDP exchange may count as a connection. The memo advises testers to measure performance by forwarding rate and sustained connections, not by the number of users.
sections.plainLanguage: Forwarding rate counts allowed bits that reach the right interface, not dropped or retransmitted bits. Connection measurements describe how many exchanges the firewall maintains and how long setup or teardown takes.

sections.title: Security and Performance Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC warns that the configuration with the best performance may not provide the best security, and vice versa. Denial-of-service traffic can prevent a firewall from forwarding allowed traffic; the memo notes that even a small amount of rejected traffic may degrade performance or stop a firewall.

Safeguards against attacks can also reduce performance. The memo does not define specific attacks because the range changes, but says benchmarks should consider safeguards and keep them in place when comparing firewalls.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall's speed and its security safeguards can affect each other. Comparisons should use the same safeguards on each firewall being tested.

viz.caption: Three traffic categories in firewall benchmarking

items.title: Allowed
items.text: The rules permit it and the firewall forwards it.

items.title: Rejected
items.text: The firewall drops it because of the rule set.

items.title: Illegal
items.text: The rules say to reject it, whether or not the firewall drops it.
